beats.text: The oldest papyrus texts in Egypt are a work crew's logbook.
beats.note: Pierre Tallet's team found them at Wadi al-Jarf, on the Red Sea coast, in 2013.

beats.text: It was written around 2560 BC, near the end of Khufu's reign.
beats.note: Wikipedia dates the papyri to about 2560 to 2550 BC.

beats.text: Merer, an inspector, shipped limestone by boat from Tura to Giza.
beats.note: Tallet believes the blocks were for the outer casing, though the log never says where the stones went.

beats.text: Merer reported to Ankhhaf, a nobleman and half brother of Khufu.
beats.note: Ankhhaf was overseer of Ra-shi-Khufu, the harbour at Giza.

beats.text: The crew ate meat, poultry, fish and beer.
beats.note: Smithsonian Magazine reports that they were well provisioned. Mark Lehner's digs at Giza uncovered apartment blocks that might have housed as many as 20,000 people.

beats.text: The oldest paperwork in Egypt is about moving stone and feeding the crew.
